newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-South Korea eyes drop in oil needs.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-South Korea eyes drop in oil needs.

text.p: Rocked by the last two oil price shocks, South Korea hopes to dramatically reduce its dependence on oil in favour of alternative energy sources including nuclear, coal and natural gas, a senior official of the Korea Gas Union said on Friday.
Over the next 13 years 19 new nuclear power stations and 29 coal fired generation plants are scheduled to be built, Ho-Kyong Kim, general secretary of Korea Gas Union told Reuters.
Korea is also seeking to increase its imports of natural gas where possible to further ofset a decline in oil usage, he said.
"In 1979 when the second shock hit, Korea's oil dependence was only 63 percent and the next year our GNP was minus 3.7 percent," Kim said.
"But now our oil imports are four times that of 1979, so if there is another shock it will have an even greater impact on the Korean economy," he told Reuters in an interview.
South Korea consumed the equivalent of about one billion tonnes of oil in 1995, 97 percent of which was imported.
Oil accounted for 62.5 percent of the total, nuclear 11.1 percent, coal 18.7 percent, liquefied natural gas 6.1 percent and hydro power and other sources accounted for the rest.
South Korea's need for primary energy by 2010 will be nearly two times greater than 1995, Kim said.
By 2010 Korea hopes to have its dependence on oil reduced to about 51 percent, a figure Kim said could still be too high.
"It is very risky for Korea to depend on oil for half its energy," Kim earlier told an energy conference here.
Nuclear power is considered one of the best energy sources for Korea although the stations could face resistance from residents, Kim said.
